verdicts.title: with_restarts reuses the name transition_steps for the total span across all cycles, silently double-specifying the length against the base schedule it wraps
verdicts.reasoning: The arithmetic reproduces exactly (`with_restarts(linear_schedule(1.0,0.0,10), 5, 3)` -> [1.0, 0.9, 0.967, 0.867, 0.933, 0.833, 0.833, ...]), but the behavior is the documented contract, not a defect. (1) `WithRestarts.__doc__` (_with_restarts.py:16-31) states 'Each cycle has (real-valued) length transition_steps / num_cycles; within a cycle, schedule is evaluated at the cycle-local position' and 'after the final cycle, returns schedule(cycle_length)'. (2) docs/reference/schedules.md:316-343 repeats this and adds the explicit instruction 'Configure `schedule` to produce its full curve over a single cycle of that length', followed by a worked SGDR example that sets `inner = cosine_schedule(1e-3, 0.0, transition_steps=1000)` with `with_restarts(inner, transition_steps=4000, num_cycles=4)`. (3) docs/user-guide/lr-scheduling.md:139-158 shows the same pairing and even names the intermediate `cycle_length = N / k`. So the coupling is not something 'a direct caller has to rediscover' from the trainer source - it is stated in the reference page, the user guide, and the class docstring, each with the correct composition spelled out. (4) The proposed validation is not implementable in general: `Schedule` is a bare `Callable[[int], float]` type alias (_schedule.py:16), not a protocol with a length attribute; several supported inners (constant_schedule, exponential/inverse_sqrt where `transition_steps` means a timescale or decay period, or any user lambda) have no 'full curve length' to compare against, so a duck-typed check would fire spuriously or not at all. (5) The 'overloaded name' premise is also weak: in `with_warmup` and in every recipe, `transition_steps` is the length of the interval that object governs; for `with_restarts` the governed interval is the whole restart window, which is consistent rather than a redefinition. (6) Behavior is pinned by tests (packages/opaque-engine/tests/scheduling/test_scheduling.py:369-411 including `test_after_window_returns_cycle_end`) and by HF-parity tests at :480-510; the only in-repo consumer (_scheduler.py:203-221) composes correctly and deliberately preserves a fractional inner span for HF parity. No privacy surface: schedules only scale the learning rate, never sensitivity, noise, or accounting inputs, so affects_epsilon=false is correct. Nothing in issues-open.tsv covers LR scheduling. Net: a documented-usage ergonomics preference (add an optional cycle-length assertion), not a defect an engineer should be dispatched to fix.
verdicts.corrected_failure_scenario: No defect established. A caller who passes an inner schedule whose own span differs from `transition_steps / num_cycles` gets a truncated or over-extended curve per cycle, e.g. `with_restarts(cosine_schedule(1.0,0.0,1000), transition_steps=1000, num_cycles=4)` yields four windows traversing only the first quarter of the cosine (values 1.0 -> 0.855 across each 250-step window) and a flat 0.8536 tail from step 1000. But this is the behavior the class docstring, docs/reference/schedules.md:316-343 and docs/user-guide/lr-scheduling.md:139-158 all document, each showing the correct pairing (`inner` built with `transition_steps = total / num_cycles`); the correctly composed form was verified to give the intended SGDR shape (1.0, 0.5, 0.0 per 250-step cycle). No generic guard is possible because `Schedule` is a plain `Callable[[int], float]` with no length attribute, and several supported inner recipes have no comparable span. Utility-only in any case; no effect on sensitivity, noise, or accounting.
